newsitem.title: USA: DLR ENDS HIGHER AS US STOCKS/BONDS REVERSE LOSSES.
newsitem.headline: DLR ENDS HIGHER AS US STOCKS/BONDS REVERSE LOSSES.

text.p: The dollar closed higher on Monday after U.S. financial markets regained their composure in the wake of Friday's massive selloff.

Traders voiced relief that U.S. assets did not repeat Friday's harrowing declines. Instead Wall Street managed gains late in the session, ending morning weakness that put the brakes on a dollar advance overseas.
"The bond market turned around and that turned around the stock market and the dollar went right up with it," said Bob Near, a vice president of foreign exchange sales at Bank of New York.

Aiding the late rally was a wire service interview with Federal Reserve Governor Susan Phillips, traders said. The report claimed that Phillips and other Fed policy makers had "hinted" they might refrain from raising interest rates, despite a strong U.S. economy.
The Dow Industrials closed up 31 points, after slipping more than 65 points during the day. The 30-year Treasury bond trimmed its losses to end up a touch.
The dollar ended trade at 1.8625/35 marks, up from 1.8563/68 at the open and 1.8450/60 at Friday's close.
It closed at 116.10/15 yen, up from a starting quote of 115.83/88 and 114.75/85 at the end of trade on Friday.
The dollar also rose to 1.5248/58 Swiss francs after kicking off trade at 1.5185/95.

The rebound started overnight. Investors in the Far East and Europe found the dollar too cheap to resist, speculating Friday's decline was only a temporary retreat from the rally which reached a near-eight-year high against the mark and a three-month peak versus the yen early last week.

Dollar/yen was bolstered by a huge decline in Japanese shares. The greenback was also heartened that European bourses regained their footing after stumbling in the wake of Friday's 157 point Dow fall and the 1-1/2 point slump in the T-bond.

"I really think it was just the stabler tone, probably helped a little bit by the more stable tone in European asset markets, and then the U.S. following that," said Bob Lynch, a currency strategist at Paribas in New York.
"There hasn't been any real follow through on selling from Friday ... for the time being it's clearly contributed to a more stable, less active tone for the dollar," he added.
Japan's Nikkei-225 stock index fell almost 4.0 percent on Monday, but shares on the London, Frankfurt and Paris exchanges mostly worked their way out of big early deficits.
Activity was light during the session amid a paucity of news and with no major U.S. data scheduled until Wednesday, when July producer prices and retail sales are released.

As is often the case during the peak summer holiday period, many dealers preferred the safety of the sidelines, at least until after the German central bank signals its intentions on interest rates at its weekly money market operation on Tuesday.

Before adjourning in July for its four-week summer recess, the Bundesbank fanned speculation that it might allow its fixed repo rate to float to stem the mark's steady decline. But a weak German economy may be a restraint on allowing the market to set the key money market rate higher.

"Given their domestic economic situation they don't want a weak deutschemark but the deutschemark weakening as it has helped their competitive advantage, so I don't think they are going to do anything," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago. .
Elsewhere, the pound rose to $1.5918/28 from $1.5895/05 and the Australian dollar rose to $0.7375/80 from $0.7371/76.
The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3930/35.
((--Alden Bentley, 212 859 1667))
